unit.title: Subjunctive with conjunctions
unit.subtitle: cuando, para que, aunque and the future

grammar.title: When time and purpose flip the verb
grammar.intro: Some little connectors pull the subjunctive along with them. The trick is time: with cuando, hasta que, and en cuanto, use the subjunctive when you point at the future (something that hasn't happened yet), but the indicative for habits. A few connectors — para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que — take the subjunctive every single time. And aunque flips to subjunctive when you're conceding a possibility.

sections.heading: cuando / hasta que / en cuanto + the future
sections.body: When these time words point to a future action that hasn't happened yet, the verb goes subjunctive. Think “whenever it eventually happens”:

sections.heading: cuando + indicative for habits
sections.body: But if cuando describes something you do routinely, it stays in the normal indicative. Habit, not future:

ex.en: When I get home, I eat.
When I get home, I'll eat.

sections.heading: Always subjunctive: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que
sections.body: These four never take the indicative. Purpose, “before”, “without”, and “unless” always point to something unrealised:

ex.en: I'll explain it so that you understand it.
Let's leave before it starts to rain.

sections.heading: aunque — concession
sections.body: Aunque takes the subjunctive when you concede something as a possibility (“even if”). Use the indicative when it's a known fact (“even though”):

ex.en: Even if it rains, we'll go to the beach.
Even though it's raining, I go out to run.

takeaways: cuando / hasta que / en cuanto + subjunctive when it's the future: Cuando llegues, llámame.
cuando + indicative for habits: Cuando llego a casa, como.
para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que → always subjunctive.

mistakes.why: A future action after 'cuando' takes the subjunctive: llegues, not llegas.

mistakes.w: Te lo digo para que vienes.
mistakes.r: Te lo digo para que vengas.
mistakes.why: 'para que' always takes the subjunctive: vengas, not vienes.

mistakes.w: Salgamos antes de que empieza a llover.
mistakes.r: Salgamos antes de que empiece a llover.
mistakes.why: 'antes de que' always takes the subjunctive: empiece, not empieza.

exercises.prompt_en: When you get home, call me.
exercises.no: A future action after 'cuando' takes the subjunctive: “llegues”.

exercises.prompt: Cuando ___ a casa, siempre como. (todos los días)
exercises.prompt_en: When I get home, I always eat. (every day)
exercises.no: A habit after 'cuando' stays in the indicative: “llego”.

exercises.prompt: Build: “I'll explain it so that you understand it.”
exercises.no: “Te lo explico para que entiendas” — 'para que' always takes the subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: Salgamos antes de que ___ a llover. (empezar)
exercises.prompt_en: Let's leave before it starts to rain.
exercises.no: 'antes de que' always takes the subjunctive → “empiece”.

exercises.prompt: Match each connector to its meaning.

exercises.translation: As soon as I can, I'll write to you.
exercises.no: It was: “En cuanto pueda, te escribo.” (As soon as I can, I'll write to you.)

exercises.scenario: Planning a beach trip despite the forecast 🏖️

exercises.no: For a possibility, use 'aunque' + subjunctive: “Aunque llueva, iremos a la playa.” (Even if it rains, we'll go.)
